bib.title: Scaling Small Agents Through Strategy Auctions

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Scaling Small Agents Through Strategy Auctions" (SALE), Lisa Alazraki, William F. Shen, Yoram Bachrach, Akhil Mathur (Meta Superintelligence Labs, Imperial, Cambridge). Preprint, arXiv:2602.02751v3 [cs.MA], dated 23 June 2026 (v3 stamped 20 Jun 2026). No venue stated.
COVERAGE: 204,339 chars extracted. I read the main text (about 1,000 lines) in full. In the appendix I read B, D, E.5, F, G, H.1, I, J, K (opening) and M. I skimmed or skipped the annotator guidelines (A.3-A.4), the prompts (C.4), E.1-E.4 refinement examples, the H.2 confusion matrices and L (qualitative comparisons). Those are examples and prompt text, not results. I read the references only for origins. The extraction is clean, apart from table columns being flattened.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Small agents fall behind as task complexity rises, so model size is a per-task decision.
 number: the 4B agent gets ~87%/92% of the 32B's pass@1 on the easiest tasks (deep search/coding) and 25%/17% on the hardest.
 setup: Qwen3 4B/8B/14B/32B, greedy decoding, HST-Bench (753 tasks), complexity = expert human solution time in 5 bins up to 60 min, LLM-judge pass@1.
 quote: "For deep search, the cheapest agent attains only 25% of the most expensive agent's pass@1 on these tasks; for coding, it reaches just 17%."
 where: Sec 4, p5 (offset ~13k)
2. Larger agents do not pay for themselves with shorter traces on hard tasks.
 number: none
 setup: same as claim 1, trace-length comparison in Fig 1b.
 quote: "larger agents do not consistently achieve shorter traces than smaller ones... the savings are too small to offset the higher per-token cost."
 where: Sec 4, p6
3. SALE beats the best single agent (Qwen3-32B) on pass@1 at lower cost.
 number: deep search 63.8 -> 67.3 pass@1 and $0.36 -> $0.21/Mt (-42%). Coding 58.4 -> 61.1 and $0.36 -> $0.27/Mt (-25%). Abstract headline: -52% reliance on the largest agent, -35% cost. The intro gives per-domain 32B workload cuts of -65% (deep search) and -40% (coding).
 setup: 4-agent pool, SALE averaged over 5 random task orderings. Baselines are single runs. Pass@1 gains are +3.5 (deep search) and +2.7 (coding). Price is a calibrated linear $/Mt: $0.05, $0.09, $0.16, $0.36 for 4B, 8B, 14B, 32B (anchored to Groq 32B pricing, 4:1 input:output ratio).
 quote: "sale reduces reliance on the largest agent by 52%, lowers overall cost by 35%, and consistently improves upon the largest agent's pass@1 with only a negligible overhead beyond executing the final trace."
 where: abstract; Table 1, p9
4. Task-description routers do worse than SALE in this setting.
 number: coding pass@1 on the hardest bin (τ≤60): WTP 6.3 vs 22.8 for the best single agent. FrugalGPT coding $0.57/Mt vs $0.36 for the best single agent. SALE is 26.1.
 setup: WTP, CARROT, TO-Router and FrugalGPT trained on the same training split. CARROT's backbone was frozen because the training set was small. Hyperparameters are in Appendix G.
 quote: "WTP achieves large savings but increasingly sacrifices pass@1 as complexity rises, dropping to 6.3% at the highest complexity versus 22.8% for the best single agent."
 where: Sec 6, p9
 caveat: WTP is cheaper than SALE on coding ($0.11 vs $0.27). CARROT ties SALE at coding τ≤0.5 (82.3 vs 82.0, p=.339).
5. The auction overhead is small, and the plan-based cost proxy is only moderately predictive.
 number: 669 extra tokens per task (deep search) and 1,042 (coding). Auction wall time 3.59 s per task vs 5-10 min to execute the trace. Strategy length vs realised trajectory length gives Spearman ρ=0.39.
 setup: 8 H100s, vLLM, 100-task stratified subset for timing.
 quote: "the auction phase represents under 1% of total token consumption."
 where: App E.5, p41. The ρ is in App D.1, p33.
6. Memory refinement shifts work to cheaper agents, and most of the effect comes from turning memory on.
 number: 32B share falls from 35% (no memory) to ~17% with memory (M>0). The 4B agent's cumulative share rises 3.7% -> 11.1% (deep search) and 1.4% -> 5.3% (coding).
 setup: 100-task leave-one-out memory ablation; Fig 5, five runs.
 quote: "enabling memory lowers 32B reliance from 35% to roughly 17% and raises refined-plan jury scores by approximately 0.3 points"
 where: App I.3, p52. Also Sec 7.3, p11.
7. The peer jury carries the value signal.
 number: without peer feedback, coding pass@1 drops to 48.7 at $0.07/Mt (vs 61.1 for full SALE). Without self-feedback, SALE sits at 64.1/58.8, close to the best single agent (63.8/58.4). Jury scores correlate with blind human plan ratings at ρ 0.74-0.82. Their point-biserial correlation with task success is only 0.36.
 quote: "peer-judgment provides the external calibration necessary for difficult problems, while self-judgment contributes efficient, low-cost signal on simpler ones."
 where: App I.2 p50-51; App J p53
8. The oracle gap remains.
 number: deep search overall oracle 77.9 pass@1 at $0.07 vs SALE 67.3; coding 68.4 vs 61.1.
 quote: "the oracle–sale gap widens (deep search τ(t) ≤ 60: 25.0 vs. 16.3; coding τ(t) ≤ 60: 34.2 vs. 26.1)."
 where: App H.1, p46
9. The largest agent still earns its place, partly through judging.
 number: no single figure; Shapley values (Table 2) show it contributes most without memory. Its coding share rises with complexity in the no-memory variant (Table 2, 65.8 at τ≤60). Its error profile also differs from the small agents' (overconfident, skips tools).
 quote: "the largest agent has the highest Shapley values across all complexity bins and task domains, even though it is not the most-selected agent in all settings"
 where: Sec 7.2, p11. Complementary failure modes: Sec 7.5, p12.

Mechanism, for the chapter: each agent writes a short plan as its bid.
- Cost is C = w_c·π(a_i)·|plan tokens|.
- Value is V = w_h·entropy + Σ w_j·(0-5 jury score from every agent, including the bidder).
- The winner is the argmin of C−V.
- Weights come from a min-max MILP on a dev set (PuLP/CBC).
- Agents cheaper than the provisional winner then rebid using retrieved win/loss plan pairs from memory.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: only two domains (deep search, coding) and one model family (Qwen3 4-32B, about an 8x price spread, below frontier models). No 70B+ models.
- Cost counts tokens only; tool calls are not priced (a tool-latency extension is only simulated in App D.5). Latency is out of scope.
- The memory bank grows linearly. Large-scale retrieval, model-version upgrades and distribution shift are untested.
- Cross-family evidence is "preliminary": Gemma 3 (100 tasks) and Llama 3.1 8B / Ministral 3 8B as bidders only, with the jury unchanged (App M).
- My observations: "auction" is a metaphor. There are no payments or incentive-compatibility analysis, and a central scorer picks the winner. The "best single agent" baseline is Qwen3-32B, not a frontier model, and the 5-run SALE averages are compared with single-run baselines. SALE needs a dev set to fit its MILP weights (so it is not entirely training-free), and the baselines were trained on small data. Gains are a few points (+2.7 to +3.5 overall).

CODE: none (the appendix gives a MILP in prose and the formulas above). The benchmark is released at github.com/facebookresearch/hst-bench.

FIGURES: Fig 3 (p8) is the single best candidate. It plots pass@1 against $/Mt per complexity bin for the 4 single agents and SALE, in deep search and coding. It shows SALE above the near-linear single-agent scaling line in every bin, which is the "routing beats the best single model at matched cost" claim at a glance. Fig 2 (p3) is the pipeline diagram if a mechanism picture is needed.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. Tables are flattened in the extraction, so the Table 1 column order (Best single, WTP, CARROT, TO-Router, FrugalGPT, SALE w/o memory, SALE) was inferred from the caption. Figure axes are unreadable as text. I did not run the figure-caption script.
